title: Stealth startup Accomplish discloses leaky-sandbox flaws in Claude Code, Codex, and Cursor
subtitle: Researchers say AI coding agents write config files inside their sandbox that trusted host software later executes — a structural gap, not a single bug, that took vendors up to 50 days to patch.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Stealth startup Accomplish disclosed a set of sandbox-escape vulnerabilities across the major AI coding agents this week, after quietly flagging them to Anthropic, OpenAI, and Cursor over the summer. The attacks do not break the sandboxes directly. Instead, the AI agent writes a configuration file inside its sandbox — a Claude hook, a Cursor MCP config, a Codex helper — that trusted software on the host machine later processes with the user's full privileges. One Cursor-side variant was assigned CVE-2026-48124 and fixed in version 3.0.0. According to Accomplish, one vendor's fix took fifty days from initial report.

The mechanism is worth understanding because it is not a bug in the model. It is a bug in the trust boundary. Every AI coding agent runs in some form of restricted environment — a container, a namespace, a permissions prompt — precisely so that a hallucinated or attacker-manipulated command cannot touch the host. But the same agent is expected to configure its own tooling, and those config files are read back by processes that live outside the sandbox. The result is a class of vulnerability where the sandbox holds, but the file the sandbox produced still owns you.

This is the second wave of AI-agent security research in as many weeks. Cymulate documented the same pattern in April as 'Configuration-Based Sandbox Escape' across Claude Code, Gemini CLI, and Codex CLI. Manifold Security's GitSpawn disclosure showed how a malicious .git config could hijack Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and Grok agents through untrusted repositories. VentureBeat's coverage frames it bluntly: every attacker went for the credential and the config file, not the model. The pattern is that AI coding agents are less secure than the sandboxes they run in — because the sandbox is not where the vulnerability lives.

For learners, especially anyone writing code with an AI agent open in another window: assume the agent is not fully sandboxed until you have read its docs and understood what it can write and where. If you clone a repository you do not fully trust, do it in a container that cannot see your ssh keys, your git credentials, or your cloud tokens. The productivity gains from AI coding tools are real, but the threat model has shifted. Learning to work inside disposable environments is now part of the craft.
